title: Snow day
text:
The snow began just after midnight, and by morning the whole city had stopped. No buses ran. The schools were closed. The radio announcer, sounding almost cheerful, advised everyone to stay at home unless their journey was absolutely essential. For the first time in eleven years, Piotr had nowhere he needed to be.

He did not know what to do with this. For eleven years, his days had been arranged with the precision of a railway timetable: the 6.15 alarm, the 7.02 tram, the meetings, the emails that arrived faster than he could answer them, the evening calls with clients in other time zones. He had been, by any reasonable measure, successful. He had also, he realised now, standing in his socks in the silent kitchen, not looked out of his own window in daylight for months.

The street below was unrecognisable. The parked cars had become soft white hills. A man was walking down the middle of the road – the middle of the road! – with a small child on his shoulders, both of them laughing. Further along, a group of teenagers had abandoned any pretence of being too old for snowball fights.

Piotr made coffee and sat at the window. His phone buzzed twice on the table behind him, then a third time. He did not turn around. He watched an old woman from the building opposite step carefully out of her door, look at the snow with an expression of deep suspicion, and then, slowly, begin to clear a path with a broom that was much too small for the job.

He finished his coffee. Then, without quite deciding to, he put on his boots and coat, found a shovel in the cellar that he could not remember buying, and went downstairs.

The woman looked up as he approached. "You're from the fourth floor," she said. It was not a question. "You always walk very fast."

"Not today," Piotr said.

They worked for an hour, side by side, mostly in silence. When the path was finished, she invited him in for tea, and he accepted, and stayed for two hours listening to her talk about the winter of 1979, when the snow had reached the first-floor windows and nobody had cared about anything except bread and coal.

That evening, the radio announced that the roads would be cleared by morning and life would return to normal. Piotr listened, nodded, and set his alarm for 6.15. Then, after a moment's thought, he changed it to 7.00.
